newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Spain markets hit by dollar fall, EMU jitters.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Spain markets hit by dollar fall, EMU jitters.

text.p: Spanish financial markets came under pressure on Tuesday, jolted by a slide in the dollar and comments that Germany might not meet the criteria for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), analysts said.
"The movements in the dollar against the mark and yen have affected practically all the markets," said one trader.

The recently buoyant dollar dropped in early trading after Germany's top economic research institutes said slight monetary tightening was possible in Germany if growth in money supply stayed above target levels.
The comments undermined Spanish bonds, shares and the peseta which had recently been supported by strong gains in U.S. markets and hopes that German interest rates would continue to fall.

The institutes also put a question mark over Germany's entry into EMU when they said Europe's leading economy would fail to meet strict debt and deficit criteria in 1997. The prospect of Germany failing to enter EMU boosted the mark further against the peseta.
Next year is the key year for deciding what countries will participate in EMU at its scheduled start in January 1999.
With the dollar the main driving factor for Spanish markets, analysts were focusing on a run of U.S. economic data this week which could add to market jitters.
"This week we've got some important data from the U.S. and their effect on the dollar will be fundamental," said one dealer.

The run of statistics on the world's biggest economy started with moderate third-quarter employment cost figures which showed a rise of 0.6 percent compared with analysts' forecasts of a 0.8 percent increase.
The U.S. consumer confidence index fell to 106.2 in October from a revised 111.9 in September, prompting a rally in U.S. Treasuries.

The figures failed to unsettle the dollar and Spanish markets but analysts said they were looking to Wednesday's preliminary third-quarter U.S. gross domestic product data and October payrolls figures due on Friday for further inspiration.
The dollar, which had come close to 115 yen overnight, weakened after tumbling through key support at 1.5160 against the mark in early European trade.
The peseta and Spanish bonds slipped through key support levels in the U.S. currency's wake.

"We've broken strong resistance at 84.30 (to the mark) and now we're heading for 84.50," one trader said earlier. "84.50 should hold for the time being but that depends of course on whether the dollar falls much further," said another dealer.

Traders said they expected the Bank of Spain would try to brake the peseta's fall if it weakened much further, intervening at around 84.45. Other analysts said 85.00 peseta/mark was a more realistic level.

"The Bank of Spain is unlikely to defend the peseta at these levels as it will be delighted to see a weakening in the currency toward 85.00 or even 86.00," said Juan Antonio Mielgo, economist at Bank of America in Madrid.

By late afternoon the peseta had recovered fractionally and was trading around 84.32/35 per mark, compared with the 84.40 level it had maintained for much of the morning. But it remained below Monday's closing levels of 82.20/22.
The spread between 10-year Spanish bonds and their German counterparts widened to 179 basis points from 172 late on Monday.
Shares managed to claw back some of their earlier losses so that the Ibex-35 stock index closed down 31.44 points or 0.72 percent at 4,352.18 after touching a low of 4,338.10 earlier.
